actSpeakBrief: Giving directions out loud is the fastest way to find out whether you can follow them.
actSpeak1: Using the plan, describe a route past four of the six points. Your partner writes the letters in order, without seeing which you chose. Compare, then swap.
actSpeak2: Do it again, but send your partner back to the junction halfway through. That reversal is the move that costs marks in the real test.
actSpeak3: Describe your own street to your partner as if it were a plan. They sketch it. Then check the sketch against a map on your phone.
actWriteBrief: Write the directions a warden would give: from the car park, past four of the lettered points, ending at point F, at the far end of the east path. Then read it aloud and time it — around 150 words a minute is the pace of the real recording.
resStrong: Strong work — the rule has landed.
resMid: Solid start. Worth one more pass.
resLow: Review the language focus slides, then try again.
coverSub: Forty questions, heard once, no pausing. The rules, the question types, and the ways candidates lose marks they had already won.
s1Title: Four sections, forty questions, one hearing
s1ColA: Four sections, ten questions each, one mark apiece. Sections 1 and 2 are everyday situations; 3 and 4 are study and lectures. The recording runs about thirty minutes.
s1ColB: You hear it once. You cannot pause it, rewind it, or ask for it again. And you will hear a range of accents, on purpose — coping with them is part of what is being tested.
s1Note: One test for Academic and General Training, marked identically. Nothing on this page changes depending on which module you are sitting.
s2Title: One difference, and it is the clock
s2ColA: On paper. You write on the question paper as you listen, then get ten minutes at the end to copy your answers onto the answer sheet. Only the answer sheet is marked.
s2ColB: On screen. You type straight in, and you get two minutes at the end to check. Then the screen locks.
s2Note: That is the only difference between the two. Same recording, same questions, same marking. If you are on paper, those ten minutes are not spare time — they are the transfer, and people run out of them.
s3ColA: Completion. Sentence, summary, form, note, table, flow-chart: six forms of one task, a gap you fill.
s3ColB: Labelling. A diagram, or a map or plan. You match a name to a position.
s3ColC: Multiple choice. Sometimes one answer from three, sometimes two from five.
s3ColD: Matching and short answer. Options A–G matched to speakers or items — a Section 3 favourite — or a question answered in the words you heard.
s3Note: The instructions change within a section. A word limit that applied to questions 1–5 may not apply to 6–10, and the limit is printed above each set, not once at the top.
s5Title: The letter that costs a mark
s6Note: Six lettered points, and a voice walking past all of them. Orient yourself before the recording starts. Marks are lost here by losing your place, not by missing a word.
s7Title: Follow the directions to a letter
s7Ctx: Click a direction on the left, then the point on the plan it describes.
s8Ctx: Write what you would put on the answer sheet, not what you heard.
s11Ctx: One of Sections 1 to 3, start to finish. Click the parts in order.
s13Title: Read the instruction, not the question
s13Ctx: Two answers that break their own instruction. Write the version that would score.
s14Title: The thirty seconds before it starts
branchLocked: Your ledger does not support this ending
x06a: That reads and/or as or. The number is allowed on top of the words, so two words plus a number is inside the limit.
x06b: Correct — that is the whole permitted set. Writing fewer words than the limit is never penalised; writing one more is marked wrong even if the meaning is right.
x06c: Two words is the ceiling, not the target. A one-word answer that is right scores exactly the same as a two-word one.
x06d: The number is extra, not one of the two words: 15 main courses is two words and a number, and it is inside the limit.
x07a: It is not a spelling error. The word is spelled correctly — it is the wrong grammatical form, which is a different fault and just as fatal.
x07b: Meaning is not the test. A grammatically wrong answer is marked wrong even where a human reader would understand it perfectly.
x07c: A missing s is one of the commonest marks lost on the whole paper. Listen for the plural, and check for it again in the transfer time.
x07d: There is no half mark anywhere in the Listening test. Every answer is one mark or nothing at all.
x09a: Note what the two right at the junction directions have in common: both send you back to the junction first. A speaker who describes one branch and then returns to describe the other is the standard shape of a map task, and following it as a single continuous walk is how candidates lose two marks at once.
x10a: 7731. Double and treble are used constantly in phone numbers and almost never taught. Hear double, write the digit twice.
x10b: 8.15. Times are safest as digits — fewer words, fewer spellings to get wrong, and always inside the word limit.
x11a: There is nothing to go back for — the recording does not repeat, and every second spent on 14 is a second of 15 you are not hearing.
x11b: Stopping to think costs you the next question too. One missed answer becomes three, and that is the real damage.
x11c: Right idea, wrong moment. Guess in the transfer time at the end, when it costs nothing — not now, when it costs question 15.
x11d: Let it go and move to 15. Then guess 14 in the transfer time — never leave a blank, because there is no penalty for a wrong answer and a blank cannot score.
x12a: It is marked wrong. When a word is spelled aloud the examiner is testing exactly that, and there is no allowance for a near miss.
x12b: There is no such tolerance anywhere in the marking. One letter out is one mark gone.
x12c: Both spellings are accepted for words that genuinely have two forms, but that is not the same as accepting an error in a name that was dictated to you.
x12d: Capitals are not required and never penalised. Writing everything in capitals is in fact a sensible habit on paper — but it will not rescue a wrong letter.
x13a: The reading time before each half is the most under-used thirty seconds in the paper. Read the questions and predict the answer type — a number? a name? a plural noun? — and you are listening for something specific instead of listening in general.
x14a: Section 1 is the most predictable part of the paper — names, numbers, dates, prices. It is where a prepared candidate should drop nothing at all.
x14b: Section 4 is a single voice, academic, and — unlike every other section — it has no pause in the middle. Ten questions, one unbroken run.
x14c: Three speakers make attribution harder, and Section 3 is genuinely difficult — but it still gets the mid-section pause that Section 4 does not.
x14d: Section 2 is a single voice on an everyday topic, and it is usually where map and plan questions appear. Harder than 1, not the hardest.
x15a: Pool. The counts as a word, and so does swimming. Three words where one was allowed scores nothing, however right it is.
x15b: C — the letter, not the word. If the instruction asks for a letter, library is a wrong answer however right it is — and this is a real and common way to lose five marks in one block.
x16a: Reading them through once is the minimum, not the plan. You will read them again anyway while the speaker talks.
x16b: Predict the kind of answer each gap wants — a number, a day, a plural noun, a name. Then you are listening for something specific, which is a far easier task than listening for everything.
x16c: Underlining every keyword leaves you with a page of underlining and no priorities. It feels productive and changes nothing.
x16d: The answers are in the order you will hear them, so working backwards buys nothing — and the last question is the one you have most time to prepare for later.
